I love Saint Nicholas.  

Saint Nicholas, good holy man,  
put on your finest robe  
and ride with it to Spain,  
bring apples from Oranges,  
plums from Damascus,  
give the little children something.  

Sinterklaas, that good lord,  
comes back every year,  
with his little horses before his wagon,  
thus Sinterklaas comes rushing in.  

3.  
You also grew in virtue over the years,  
veiling the sins of youthful youth,  
diligently seeking knowledge,  
you became accomplished in it in a short time.  

4.  
During Lent you tamed your body,  
the flesh stung with a hairy garment restrained;  
your soul, a temple of the Holy Spirit,  
was attached to God day and night.  

5.

you diligently cultivated virtue even further,  
your body waged a heavy war,  
so that it would be more subject to the spirit.  

6.  
You slept and ate much less than before,  
and your drink was clear water alone,  
your clothes were poor, yet neat,  
the spirit always cared for in prayer.  

7.  
When both your parents were dead,  
you received a very large inheritance from them,  
which you did not squander uselessly  
or lock away in an iron chest.

You gave to the poor generously,  
because you did not consider yourself the owner,  
but as a distributor appointed by the Lord,  
through which this deed of yours is also told:

which was deadly evil for their souls,  
that for a piece of money they would taint  
their purity with dishonor.

threw a bag of gold through the window,  
which was kept by one daughter.

by which the second daughter was married,  
such great power had this hidden gold.

by which he saved her body from need  
and her soul from death.

you know our slippery state,  
through which our inconsiderate young youth

["Listen, Friends and understand well,  
Hear this Song,  
Always abundant from the Fisherman,  
And also its use,  
For no City in the Netherlands  
Can do without it.  
There is scarcely a trade common,  
Large or small,  
That the Fisherman cannot see suffer,  
Few merchants praised,  
Unless goods from it  
Are found on the Ship.  
The Merchant ship brings Chalk and Grease,  
Also Pitch and Tar,  
Which the Fisherman first needs  
For his Ship without fail,  
Many a Skipper also goes away  
To fetch hemp.  
From this one makes Ropes and Cords  
Very abundantly,  
Many ships certainly sail to Spain,  
To get Salt from there,  
Wherewith he carries salt, Herring and Fish,  
Without fail,  
He addresses the Shipbuilder  
Before all men,  
Who makes his Ship masts well,  
To build for the Sea,  
Because he wants to complete his Journey  
With speed.  
The Smith generally makes Anchors,  
Builds large and small,  
The Block-maker also comes in handy,  
In various affairs,  
He must skillfully make Blocks, Pumps, and Compasses.  
The Line carriers also in the trade,  
Make many Ropes,  
And Cables for the Fisherman's Ship,  
So that it does not get caught  
In Storm and distress, on Sand or Rock,  
In these matters.  
The Sailmaker also makes  
His Sails ready;  
And the Cooper makes from split wood  
Large and small Barrels,  
In which he stores Herring and Fish in salt  
For his benefit.  
The Basket maker very pushy  
Makes from Rushes,  
Baskets, Traps, and good Holders,  
In which the Fisherman proudly  
Puts various fresh Fish,  
Skewers to keep alive.  
The Baker, Brewer, Grocer  
Know very well,  
That they have to do with the Fisherman,  
And the Shoemaker nicely  
Makes the Fisherman Clauses and Shoes,  
Worthy of praise.  
To the Cloth merchant in the season,  
He has much to do,  
Then the Tailor is addressed,  
Could I even imagine it all,  
How many a Workman  
Must earn his living.  
Few can harm the Fisherman,  
Even the Merchant,  
He buys Herring and Fish boldly,  
Sends them to various Countries,  
Then goods are obtained abundantly,  
In many ways.  
Also the Fisherman certainly brings you,  
Various kinds of Fish,  
With which many of their livelihood go,  
Skippers, Merchants, well-wishers,  
Simply the Fisherman is therefore loved  
By all People.  
He brings you the noble fine Herring,  
Cod done well,  
Halibut, Haddock, and Plaice,  
Whiting, Ling, Mackerel good,  
Also Turbot and Aberdeen,  
Abundantly.  
And still more other Fish,  
That is certain,  
The Fisherman brings you very boldly,  
To the Countryman's enjoyment,  
At his Table very abundantly,  
Good in flavor.  
Therefore do not despise the Fisherman,  
For much sorrow  
He suffers in Storms and distress,  
While the Countryman sleeps in peace,  
With his Wife and Children dear,  
As he wishes.  
See Friends this difference is great,  
Who can now earn his Bread  
Here on Land,  
Without having to sail out to Sea,  
Suffering the sorrow of Winter  
Storm and waves.  
Also he is often heavily burdened  
With a whole Journey,  
That he nevertheless enjoys no Profit,  
Yes whole Years,  
Tell me, is that not heavy sorrow,  
To sail like that.  
Mark once what gratitude you owe  
To God with diligence,  
Who lives here on Land in peace,  
Like blessed People,  
With Wife and Children to his liking  
And desire.  
Farewell Fishermen Young and Old,  
Trust in God;  
Even if you often have adversity,  
Do not therefore despair,  
You will gain Heaven's reward,  
But keep it.  
Who composed and established us this New Song,  
Was a good Fisherman from Vlaardingen,  
He was still Young in years,  
And wished the Fishermen much prosperity  
Who go to Sea.", 'Come, swift young lads,
Sailors, come aboard.
We are about to set out as privateers;
There beats the drum! Onward, onward.
The little ship is already seaworthy;
It is right before the wind and tide.
Are you still worthy of the name
Of Vlissingers, follow me!

The letters have arrived,
Look there, now we go aboard;
Now there is no shirking,
That we seize you like pirates.
Now we will show those British
Who we really are;
It will not stay like this!
Here’s a toast of wine for everyone.

To the health of the Lords of the Land,
And the Admiral-in-Chief;
May they rule us for a long time!..
I bring it to you once again.
The wine gives fire and life!
So we set sail.
Now let the ship’s bow vibrate freely
With a repeated Huzzah!

But when we get prizes,
And look, there we go for it,
We will not keep quiet about it;
Live in communion with the loot.
Treat the shipmates
As sailors should:
I forbid you to torment them,
And if you do; stand firm!

If anyone dares to exact revenge
On Scots or Englishmen,
I will speak to them
In a way they will remember; I can.
I want to repay you,
See there, there is my hand:
No cruelty adds to heroes;
He who fights, fights for his country.

Listen, I will live with you
As brothers; do not forget
That to me was given
The highest command.
The advance payment has been received,
You were satisfied with that,
It was after all your desire?
You admitted that yourself.

Cursing, swearing, and roaring,
I also dislike;
He must learn to give that up,
Who wants to stand with me.
Whoever loses themselves in drink,
Or is of bad nature,
Behold, this rope with knots
Is kept here for them.

Be cheerful, merry, jocular,
Sing so it resounds; that’s well.
Be active, orderly, lively,
This suits a shipmate.
And if it comes to fighting,
Look there, this is the man
Who will judge you,
If you get the worse of it.

You will not lack courage
When it comes to striking:
I do not want to speak a word of it;
I see you as men.
But now that we speak of it,
In round sailor’s speech:
Will you not abandon me?
What do you all say?
Captain! I speak for all:
Whatever we encounter on the voyage,
Wherever our fate may fall,
We will shed all our blood
With you, if necessary;
We are ready for that.
Never want to dishonor our honor:
Our word, see, that is our oath.

And are we rough men?
It is less in deed than appearance.
See there, Captain, we wish
To be at the dance already.
The blood boils in our veins
Remembering the insult...
Those pirates, those barbarians!
Now they get their due!

See there, there is mate Steven,
He sailed for Amsterdam;
Is that ever to be forgiven,
They beat him half senseless.
They bound him with ropes
To the leg; one can
Clearly see the bruises;
Who ever heard of that!

Here, Kees, the sweet boy,
Also knows that scum of a people;
They forced him,
Threatened with a bare dagger;
Because he did not want to talk,
And the boy knew no evil:
“You can cut me into pieces,
But I know of no betrayal.”

So the lad let himself be heard:
Isn’t that true, my curly-haired one?
He was born for the sea,
And goes to the ship like a madman.
There is much to expect from him.
He has a fine understanding.
If he keeps his duty,
He will get a ship someday.
Now mates, I am satisfied,
You speak as sailors should.
And Kees I take today
With me. Come, sailor guest,
I see what I can make of you;
The Rider had to watch the cabin first, like you;
And what a man he became!', "Dirty, dirty, baby!  
Porridge stands in the spinning wheel;  
Milk from the spotted cow,  
Childman, close your little eyes!  
If you do not want to be quiet,  
Then I'll get a stick  
And hit you right on your bare bottom,  
Because you start to grin.  
Come, little sweetie! sit down,  
Each on a chair,  
And give that beautiful girl  
A kiss on each cheek!  
What does Maria have on her lap?  
A little child.  
What does that child have in hand?  
A beautiful book.  
What is written inside?  
For father and mother to sleep alone,  
And I lie in a little cradle.  
The cradle can be made,  
Then I sleep in a sheet;  
The sheet is in the wash,  
Then I sleep in a puddle;  
The puddle is too deep,  
Then I sleep in the reed;  
The reed is too long,  
Then I sleep by the snake;  
The snake is too wicked,  
Then I sleep by the lizard;  
The lizard is too beautiful,  
Then I sleep in the hay.  
I’ve already been such a customer,  
I am still such a customer,  
And whoever has something to say about it,  
Can just come up with it.  
A hat with plumes!  
A skirt made of parchment.  
The whole city is burned down  
All because of that crazy man.  
Hoppelepop  
My little bread is gone.  
My little bag is to the mill.  
I still have a little penny,  
That’s not a cent too much.  
One, two, three, four, five, six, seven.  
Jan van den Beld came by  
Already with a basket on his back.  
What was that little basket worth?  
Two golden pins.  
A little coal fire,  
A little coal fire  
Is already too expensive.  
Then give me a slap on the head,  
A slap on the head hurts too much,  
Just give me both little ears again!  
They came last  
Alone in a wooden tub.  
Soapwood!  
Beat on a bone,  
Beat on an ash or two,  
I will throw you into the sea again.  
If you then come ashore,  
I will throw you with sand.  
If you then come onto the dike again,  
I will throw you into the mud.  
Whole or half!  
Just bite the head off the beetle!  
What is needed?  
A little coal fire.  
I have no fire.  
I saw your chimney smoking, though.  
That was at the neighbor’s.  
May I come in briefly?  
Too dirty clogs.  
Take off clogs?  
Too dirty pants.  
Pull off pants?  
Too dirty feet.  
Wash the feet?  
First put on the pretty little shoes.  
Wife, how your house looks!  
Get a broom and clean it out!  
What beautiful children do you have!  
It suits you quite well!  
May I have one of them?  
What will you give them to eat?  
All the treats that I have.  
Then just give her one!  
In a while I will bring you a pot of snakes!  
Go away, you ugly witch!  
Spin, spin, Lisje!  
Every day a little pile,  
Every day a little web,  
That goes towards Lisje’s dress.  
In Voassen already on the Rollekoord,  
Haven’t you heard about it?  
Of three pretty girls?  
One sat knitting,  
The other sat braiding,  
The third was spinning,  
And the very smallest little lady,  
Won the most money!  
Spin, Lisje! spin!  
The suitors are arriving.  
Little ball, little ball of yarn!  
Beautiful girl of eighteen years!  
Beautiful girl has already turned around,  
That she learned from father and mother.  
Then came Jan the butcher,  
Who said: ‘The yard was thin.’  
Then came Jan the carpenter,  
Who nailed the dog’s tail back on."]
